questions.q: Among the following, the largest and most complex animal viruses are the:
questions.x: Poxviruses (such as the smallpox virus) are large brick-shaped viruses, about 250–300 nm long. Polio-, parvo- and rhinoviruses are small icosahedral viruses.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of AIDS?
o: Diarrhoea lasting more than a month
A steady rise in the number of helper T cells
questions.x: In AIDS helper T cells fall, they do not rise. Chronic diarrhoea, night sweats, fever and weight loss are all typical signs.

questions.q: The approximate diameter of a human immunodeficiency virus particle is:
questions.x: HIV is a roughly spherical enveloped virus about 100 nm in diameter. 1 µm and 10 µm are the sizes of bacteria and body cells.

questions.q: In aerobic respiration, water is formed when:
o: Oxygen accepts electrons and protons at the end of the electron transport chain
Carbon dioxide is released in the Krebs cycle
Pyruvate is converted into acetyl CoA
questions.x: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor; it combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water. Glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle do not produce this water.

questions.q: Unlike alcoholic fermentation in yeast, lactic acid fermentation in human muscle:
questions.x: Pyruvate is reduced straight to lactic acid with no loss of carbon dioxide. Both kinds of fermentation occur in the cytoplasm, regenerate NAD+ and give the same net 2 ATP.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a monomer with a polymer built from it?
questions.x: Haemoglobin is a protein, a polymer of amino acids. Keratin is also a protein, starch is a polymer of glucose, and chitin is a polysaccharide, not a fatty acid polymer.

questions.q: Which amino acid is basic because its R group contains an extra amino group?
questions.x: Lysine has an extra –NH₂ group in its side chain, making it basic. Glycine and alanine are neutral, and glutamic acid has an extra carboxyl group, making it acidic.

questions.q: The molecular formula of a triose sugar is:
questions.x: Trioses, such as glyceraldehyde, have three carbons and fit the formula C3H6O3. C3H8O3 is glycerol, which is an alcohol, not a sugar.

questions.q: The myelin sheath that insulates many nerve fibres is rich in:
questions.x: Myelin is made of layers of cell membrane and is mostly lipid, which acts as an electrical insulator. Cellulose and glycogen are polysaccharides, and keratin is the protein of hair and nails.

questions.q: Deoxyribose, the sugar of DNA, is a:
questions.x: Deoxyribose, like ribose, is a pentose with five carbon atoms. Glucose is an example of a hexose.

questions.q: In liquid water, the hydrogen bonds between molecules are:
o: Permanent, holding each molecule in a fixed place
Absent, because they form only in ice
Covalent bonds that share electrons equally
Constantly breaking and re-forming as the molecules move
questions.x: In the liquid, molecules move about, so hydrogen bonds break and re-form very rapidly. Only in ice are they held in a fixed, regular lattice.

questions.q: In DNA, guanine pairs with cytosine by:
questions.x: A guanine–cytosine pair is held by three hydrogen bonds, while an adenine–thymine pair has two. Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides within a strand, not across it.

questions.q: In a glycoprotein, the carbohydrate chains are:
o: Held to the protein only by hydrogen bonds
Joined to the protein through a lipid tail
questions.x: The sugar chains of a glycoprotein are attached to particular amino acids of the protein by covalent bonds, so they stay firmly attached.

questions.q: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, (A + T)/(G + C) = 1.5. What percentage of its bases is guanine?
questions.x: A + T is 1.5 times G + C, so A + T = 60% and G + C = 40%. Since G = C, guanine is 20%.

questions.q: Lactose is important in the diet of young mammals because it:
o: Forms the walls of their cells
Is the main sugar of milk and supplies them with energy
Is the main protein of their muscles
questions.x: Lactose (milk sugar) is a disaccharide that young mammals digest into glucose and galactose for energy. It is not structural, a carrier or a protein.

questions.q: Water is cooled steadily from 10 °C to 0 °C. How does its density change?
o: It decreases steadily all the way to 0 °C
It increases until about 4 °C and then decreases
It increases steadily all the way to 0 °C
It stays the same until it freezes
questions.x: Water is densest at about 4 °C. Below that, hydrogen bonds begin to hold the molecules in a more open arrangement, so density falls as it approaches freezing.

questions.q: A person with the karyotype 47,XXY develops as a male. This shows that, in humans, maleness is mainly determined by:
o: The presence of a Y chromosome
questions.x: Despite having two X chromosomes, an XXY person (Klinefelter syndrome) is male, because a gene on the Y chromosome triggers male development.

questions.q: Compared with a large eukaryotic cell, a small bacterial cell has a:
o: Smaller surface area to volume ratio, so it exchanges materials slowly
Smaller ratio, so it needs no plasma membrane
Larger ratio, so it needs a nuclear envelope
Larger surface area to volume ratio, so materials are exchanged rapidly
questions.x: Small cells have more surface for each unit of volume, so diffusion can supply all of the cell quickly. Large eukaryotic cells rely on internal membranes and transport.

questions.q: Proteins made on the ribosomes of the rough ER first pass into the:
o: Lumen of the ER cisternae, where they are folded and transported
questions.x: Proteins made on RER enter the ER lumen, where they fold and may be modified before travelling in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: Chemically, the DNA of a chromosome is a polymer of:
questions.x: DNA is a long chain of deoxyribonucleotides, each made of deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate and a nitrogenous base. Ribonucleotides make up RNA.

questions.q: A typical bacterium has one circular chromosome, so with respect to its main genes it is:
questions.x: With only one copy of each main gene on its single chromosome, a bacterium is haploid. Most body cells of plants and animals are diploid.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares unconditioned and conditioned reflexes?
o: Conditioned reflexes are inherited, while unconditioned reflexes are learned
Unconditioned reflexes are similar in all members of a species, while conditioned reflexes differ between individuals
Unconditioned reflexes need training to form, while conditioned reflexes do not
Both types are permanent and can never fade
questions.x: Unconditioned reflexes are inborn and common to the whole species. Conditioned reflexes depend on each individual's experience, so they differ from person to person and can fade if not reinforced.

questions.q: A person stops noticing a wristwatch soon after putting it on, although it still presses on the skin. This is mainly because the touch receptors:
o: Are destroyed by the continued pressure
Send their impulses only to the spinal cord
Adapt, sending fewer impulses to an unchanging stimulus
questions.x: Many receptors adapt: with a constant stimulus their impulse frequency falls, so the sensation fades. The receptors are not damaged and still respond to any new change.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential of a neuron is a potential difference across its:
questions.x: The resting potential exists across the plasma membrane because of the unequal distribution of ions inside and outside the cell.

questions.q: Which pair of responses are BOTH unconditioned reflexes?
o: The knee jerk and a dog salivating at a dinner bell
Coughing and a child crying at the sight of a syringe
Blinking and stopping a car at a red signal
questions.x: Sneezing and the knee jerk are inborn and need no learning. Salivating at a bell, fearing a syringe and stopping at a red signal are all learned through experience, so each wrong pair contains one conditioned response.

questions.q: The sodium–potassium pump moves ions across the neuron membrane by:
questions.x: The pump moves Na+ and K+ against their concentration gradients, which needs energy from ATP: this is active transport.

questions.q: The neurotransmitter released at the junctions between motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres is:
questions.x: Motor neurons are cholinergic: they release acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions. Noradrenaline is released by most sympathetic endings.

questions.q: Impulses of which sense reach the cerebral cortex WITHOUT first being relayed in the thalamus?
questions.x: The thalamus relays almost all sensory impulses to the cortex, including vision, hearing and touch. Smell is the exception: olfactory impulses pass from the olfactory bulbs directly to the cortex.

questions.q: The cell body of a neuron has a large nucleus with a prominent nucleolus and many Nissl's granules. These features show that the cell body is very active in:
questions.x: A prominent nucleolus makes ribosomes, and Nissl's granules are rough ER with ribosomes: both point to active protein synthesis. Mature neurons do not divide.

questions.q: In germinating seeds, stored starch is converted into maltose by the enzyme:
questions.x: Amylase hydrolyses starch into maltose, supplying sugar to the growing embryo. Lipase acts on fats and pepsin on proteins.

questions.q: A drug designed to block an enzyme by fitting into its active site is usually made to resemble:
o: The product of a different enzyme
questions.x: To occupy the active site, a competitive inhibitor must have a shape and charge similar to the substrate.

questions.q: Naturally occurring enzyme inhibitors in cells help to:
questions.x: Cells use inhibition, such as feedback inhibition, to switch pathways on and off so that products are made only when needed.

questions.q: An enzyme is added to a fixed, small amount of substrate. If the experiment is repeated with twice as much enzyme, then:
o: The same total amount of product forms, but in a shorter time
Twice as much product forms in total
Half as much product forms in total
questions.x: The total product depends on the substrate available, which is unchanged. More enzyme only makes the reaction finish sooner.

questions.q: In sexually reproducing organisms, new combinations of existing alleles on which natural selection can act are produced mainly by:
o: Crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis
questions.x: Meiosis shuffles alleles through crossing over and independent assortment, and fertilisation combines them further. Mitosis copies cells without new combinations.

questions.q: According to Lamarck, a completely new organ appears in an animal because:
o: The animal feels a new need caused by a change in its surroundings
A chance variation is preserved by natural selection
A gene is copied wrongly during meiosis
The organ is created suddenly in one generation
questions.x: Lamarck held that a new need produced by a changed environment leads to new habits and so to new or altered organs. Chance variation and selection belong to Darwin's theory.

questions.q: In Lamarck's theory, the variations that lead to evolution are:
o: Random and present before any need arises
Produced in response to the needs of the organism
Caused only by errors in copying DNA
Produced only in the germ cells
questions.x: Lamarck thought variations arise purposefully, as a response to need and use. Darwin and modern genetics say variation is random and already present; selection then acts on it.

questions.q: Lamarck would explain the very small, poorly developed eyes of moles, which live underground, as the result of:
o: Use of the eyes in dim light
Disuse of the eyes over many generations
questions.x: In Lamarck's view, moles living in darkness no longer used their eyes, so the eyes shrank and this reduction was inherited.

questions.q: Which of these is a function of the vagina?
o: It is the site of fertilisation
It receives sperm during intercourse and forms the birth canal
questions.x: The vagina receives the penis and sperm and acts as the birth canal. Ova are made in the ovaries and fertilisation occurs in the oviduct.

questions.q: A woman's resting body temperature rises slightly soon after ovulation and stays higher until menstruation. This rise is caused by:
questions.x: Progesterone, secreted during the luteal phase, raises the basal body temperature by a few tenths of a degree. It falls again when the corpus luteum degenerates.

questions.q: Non-identical (fraternal) twins develop when:
o: One fertilised egg splits into two embryos
Two follicles release oocytes in the same cycle and each is fertilised by a different sperm
One oocyte is fertilised by two sperm
One follicle releases one oocyte that divides before fertilisation
questions.x: Fraternal twins come from two separate oocytes and two sperm, so they are as alike as ordinary siblings. A single zygote that splits gives identical twins.

questions.q: In an adult long bone, the shaft (diaphysis) is made mainly of:
o: Hyaline cartilage with a thin bony covering
Compact bone surrounding a marrow cavity
questions.x: The shaft is a tube of compact bone enclosing the marrow cavity. Spongy bone is mainly found in the enlarged ends (epiphyses).

questions.q: The smallest bone in the human body, found in the middle ear, is the:
questions.x: The stapes is the smallest bone. With the malleus and incus it passes sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear.

questions.q: If gout attacks keep returning over many years without control, a likely long-term result is:
o: Complete regrowth of the joint cartilage
Damage and deformity of the affected joints
Permanent loss of all uric acid from the blood
questions.x: Repeated inflammation from urate crystals gradually damages cartilage and bone, so the joints can become deformed. Cartilage does not regrow, and uric acid does not disappear from the blood.

questions.q: How many carpal bones are there in each human wrist?
questions.x: Each wrist has eight small carpal bones. Seven is the number of tarsals in the ankle, five the number of metacarpals and fourteen the number of phalanges in a hand.

questions.q: The head of the femur fits into a cup-shaped socket in the hip bone called the:
questions.x: The acetabulum of the hip bone receives the head of the femur at the hip joint. The glenoid cavity of the scapula receives the humerus.

questions.q: A patient's joint pain gets worse with use during the day and eases with rest; morning stiffness lasts only a few minutes. This pattern points most to:
questions.x: Pain that builds with use and settles with rest, with brief morning stiffness, is typical of osteoarthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis gives long morning stiffness that eases with movement, and gout and septic arthritis come on suddenly.

questions.q: Each joint between vertebral bodies allows only slight movement, yet the backbone as a whole can bend a lot. This is because:
o: Each vertebra can rotate freely like a pivot
Small movements at many joints add up
The intervertebral discs are synovial cavities
The vertebrae are not connected to one another
questions.x: The vertebral column has many slightly movable joints in a row, and their small movements add together to give a large bend. The discs are cartilage, not synovial cavities.

questions.q: Osteocytes need canaliculi to stay alive, but chondrocytes do not. The main reason is that:
o: Chondrocytes have their own blood capillaries
Bone matrix is mineralised, so substances cannot diffuse easily through it
Cartilage matrix is full of blood vessels
questions.x: The hard, calcified matrix of bone blocks diffusion, so osteocytes rely on canaliculi to reach the blood supply. The softer cartilage matrix lets nutrients diffuse through it, even though cartilage has no blood vessels.

questions.q: In the human body, which cells normally carry out crossing over?
o: Cells of the gonads undergoing meiosis to form gametes
questions.x: Crossing over happens in prophase I of meiosis, which occurs in the testes and ovaries when gametes are made. Body cells divide by mitosis, where it does not normally occur.

questions.q: A cross in which the parents differ in two pairs of contrasting characters is called a:
questions.x: A dihybrid cross follows two characters at once, such as seed shape and seed colour. A monohybrid cross follows only one character.

questions.q: The independent assortment of different homologous chromosome pairs takes place during:
o: Metaphase I and anaphase I of meiosis
questions.x: Each homologous pair lines up at metaphase I with a random orientation, and the pairs separate at anaphase I. That is when alleles of genes on different chromosomes are sorted independently.

questions.q: In an insect with the XX–XO system, the male has 23 chromosomes in his body cells. His sperm will carry:
questions.x: The male has 22 autosomes + one X. Each sperm gets 11 autosomes, and half also get the X (12) while half get no sex chromosome (11).

questions.q: The segments exchanged between non-sister chromatids during crossing over are:
o: Corresponding segments carrying alleles of the same genes
Random segments of any length from any chromosome
Segments from sister chromatids of the same chromosome
Whole arms swapped with non-homologous chromosomes
questions.x: Crossing over is a reciprocal exchange of equivalent segments between homologous non-sister chromatids, so alleles of the same genes change places. Exchange with non-homologous chromosomes would be a translocation.

questions.q: In the F2 of a dihybrid cross (AaBb × AaBb), what fraction of the offspring is homozygous for one gene and heterozygous for the other?
questions.x: For each gene, P(homozygous) = 1/2 and P(heterozygous) = 1/2. Homozygous A with heterozygous B is 1/4, and heterozygous A with homozygous B is another 1/4, so the total is 1/2.

questions.q: When crossing over does occur between two linked loci in a coupling heterozygote (AB/ab), the total number of gamete types it can produce becomes:
questions.x: Without crossing over only AB and ab form. Crossing over between the loci adds the recombinants Ab and aB, making four types, though the parental types remain more frequent.

questions.q: A man with blood group A (Iᴬi) marries a woman with blood group B (Iᴮi). Their children can have blood groups:
o: Any of the four groups: A, B, AB or O
Groups A, B and AB, but never O
questions.x: Iᴬi × Iᴮi gives IᴬIᴮ (group AB), Iᴬi (group A), Iᴮi (group B) and ii (group O), each with probability 1/4. Because both parents carry i, a group O child is possible.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the layers of the heart wall, from outside to inside?
questions.x: The thin epicardium covers the outside, the thick muscular myocardium is in the middle, and the endocardium lines the chambers.

questions.q: Unlike absorbed glucose, absorbed fats reach the general blood circulation without passing first through the liver. This is because fats:
o: Enter lacteals and travel in lymph to the veins near the neck
Are carried in the hepatic portal vein
Are absorbed directly through the stomach wall
Are broken down to glucose in the villi
questions.x: Glucose enters blood capillaries and travels in the hepatic portal vein to the liver. Fats enter lacteals and travel in the lymph to the thoracic duct, which joins a vein in the neck.

questions.q: During a severe loss of blood, the spleen can help because it:
o: Produces new plasma proteins at once
Pumps blood like a second heart
Stores a reserve of blood that it can release into circulation
questions.x: The spleen holds a reserve of blood. When blood is lost, it can contract and send this blood into the circulation.

questions.q: As blood travels from the aorta to the capillaries, its pressure falls most steeply while it passes through the:
questions.x: Arterioles are narrow and muscular and offer the greatest resistance, so the biggest pressure drop happens there. Pressure in the aorta and large arteries stays high, and the venae cavae come after the capillaries.

questions.q: When the arterioles supplying the skin widen (vasodilation) on a hot day:
o: Less blood reaches the skin and heat is kept in
More blood flows near the skin surface and more heat is lost
The heart stops pumping blood to the skin
Blood moves from the skin into the veins of the gut
questions.x: Relaxed arteriole muscle widens the vessels, sending more warm blood near the skin surface so heat is lost. Narrowing (vasoconstriction) does the opposite.

questions.q: After a B cell is activated, some of its daughter cells do not secrete antibody at once but live for years. These are:
questions.x: Memory B cells stay in the body long after the infection and respond quickly if the same antigen returns. Plasma cells secrete antibody straight away but are short-lived.

questions.q: A single plasma cell secretes antibodies that are:
o: All of one kind, specific for one antigen
Of every kind, against all antigens
Of a new kind every hour
questions.x: A plasma cell comes from one B-cell clone, so all the antibody it secretes has the same binding site and fits the same antigen.

questions.q: In the pulmonary capillaries, hydrogencarbonate ions move back from the plasma into the red blood cells. At the same time, chloride ions:
o: Move into the red blood cells with the hydrogencarbonate
Combine with haemoglobin to release oxygen
Move out of the red blood cells into the plasma
Are exhaled into the alveolar air
questions.x: In the lungs the chloride shift reverses: HCO₃⁻ enters the red cells to be turned back into CO₂, and Cl⁻ leaves to keep the charge balanced. In the tissues the movements are the other way round.

questions.q: Besides the lungs, smoking also increases the risk of cancer of the:
questions.x: Smoke and tar pass over the lining of the mouth, throat and larynx, and are swallowed into the oesophagus, so cancers of these parts are much more common in smokers.

questions.q: A patient with severe emphysema caused by smoking has a bluish colour of the lips and fingertips. This is because:
o: Tar has stained the skin blue
Too much oxygen is carried in the blood
Nicotine has widened the blood vessels of the skin
The blood leaving the lungs is poorly oxygenated
questions.x: With fewer, damaged alveoli, much less oxygen enters the blood, so a large amount of haemoglobin stays deoxygenated, giving a bluish tinge (cyanosis). Tar does not stain the lips blue.

questions.q: Bile is made by the liver all the time but is released into the gut mainly after meals. Between meals, bile travels by which route?
o: Liver → common bile duct → duodenum → gall bladder
Liver → hepatic duct → cystic duct → gall bladder
questions.x: Between meals the sphincter at the duodenal end of the common bile duct is closed, so bile from the hepatic duct backs up the cystic duct into the gall bladder for storage. After a meal it flows out through the common bile duct to the duodenum.

questions.q: Inactive pepsinogen secreted into the stomach is converted into active pepsin by:
questions.x: Hydrochloric acid from the parietal cells activates pepsinogen to pepsin, and pepsin then activates more. Enterokinase activates trypsinogen in the duodenum, and gastrin is a hormone, not an activator.

questions.q: Besides making the gall bladder contract, the hormone cholecystokinin (CCK) also stimulates the:
o: Stomach to secrete more hydrochloric acid
Pancreas to secrete a juice rich in enzymes
questions.x: CCK is released by the duodenum when fats and proteins arrive. It empties the gall bladder and makes the pancreas release enzyme-rich juice, while secretin mainly causes a watery bicarbonate juice.

questions.q: Which order shows hydrostatic blood pressure from highest to lowest?
o: Peritubular capillaries → glomerular capillaries → renal vein
Glomerular capillaries → peritubular capillaries → renal vein
Renal vein → glomerular capillaries → peritubular capillaries
Glomerular capillaries → renal vein → peritubular capillaries
questions.x: Pressure is highest in the glomerulus, drops after the resistant efferent arteriole into the low-pressure peritubular capillaries, and is lowest in the veins draining the kidney.

questions.q: A person standing in a cold wind loses heat faster than in still air at the same temperature, mainly by:
questions.x: Moving air keeps replacing the warmed layer of air next to the skin, so heat is carried away faster by convection.

questions.q: If the heat-gain centre of the hypothalamus were damaged, which responses in a cold room would most likely fail?
o: Shivering and constriction of skin arterioles
questions.x: The heat-gain centre drives the warming responses: shivering and vasoconstriction. Sweating and vasodilation are cooling responses run by the heat-loss centre.

questions.q: Besides the kidneys, which organ removes small amounts of urea, salts and water from the body?
questions.x: Sweat contains water, salts and a little urea, so the skin plays a small excretory role. The lungs excrete carbon dioxide and water vapour but not urea.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a kidney stone treatment with how it works?
o: Keyhole surgery: the stone is dissolved by drugs
Ureteroscopy: the stone is removed through a cut in the abdomen
Shock-wave lithotripsy: waves from outside the body break the stone
Open surgery: the stone is broken by waves through intact skin
questions.x: Shock-wave lithotripsy breaks the stone from outside. Keyhole surgery uses a small cut, ureteroscopy uses no cut, and open surgery uses a large cut.

questions.q: A patient confined to bed for many weeks after a fracture has a higher risk of calcium stones because:
o: Resting muscles release large amounts of uric acid
Calcium is released from the unused bones and more appears in the urine
questions.x: Bones that bear no weight lose calcium, so urine calcium rises and calcium stones form more easily.

questions.q: After several days of a very salty diet, aldosterone secretion falls. As a result the kidneys:
o: Reabsorb less sodium, so more salt is passed in the urine
Reabsorb more sodium, so less salt is passed
Stop filtering sodium at the glomerulus
Secrete more water into the PCT
questions.x: Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb sodium. When it falls, more sodium stays in the tubule and is excreted, which restores the body's salt balance.

questions.q: Which of these patients is most likely to develop chronic, rather than acute, kidney failure?
o: A woman who lost much blood in childbirth
A child severely dehydrated by diarrhoea
A man given a mismatched blood transfusion
A man with poorly controlled diabetes for 20 years
questions.x: Long-standing diabetes damages the glomeruli slowly over years, giving chronic failure. Blood loss, dehydration and mismatched transfusion cause sudden, acute failure.

questions.q: A urea molecule filtered in a glomerulus is passed out of the body in urine. Which structure does it NOT pass through?
questions.x: Filtered urea travels Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct, pelvis, ureter, bladder and urethra. The renal vein carries blood away from the kidney, not urine.

questions.q: Recombinant human insulin is used in the treatment of:
questions.x: Insulin lowers blood glucose and is given to people with diabetes mellitus whose bodies make too little insulin. Diabetes insipidus is due to lack of ADH, not insulin.

questions.q: The MMR vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella is an example of a:
o: Recombinant subunit vaccine made in yeast
questions.x: MMR contains weakened but living measles, mumps and rubella viruses. Toxoids are used against bacterial toxins such as tetanus, and the yeast-made subunit vaccine is the hepatitis B vaccine.

questions.q: Viruses for vaccine production cannot be grown on nutrient media like bacteria because they:
o: Are too large to fit on a culture plate
Are killed by the oxygen in air
Can reproduce only inside living host cells
Need sunlight to make their own food
questions.x: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites: they have no metabolism of their own and use the host cell's machinery to multiply. They are far smaller than bacteria.

questions.q: How many hydrogen atoms are present in 1.6 g of methane, CH₄? (C = 12, H = 1; Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.x: Moles of CH₄ = 1.6/16 = 0.1 mol; each molecule has 4 H atoms, so 0.4 mol H = 0.4 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 2.408 × 10²³. 6.02 × 10²² is the number of molecules, not H atoms.

questions.q: Silver nitrate solution is mixed with sodium chloride solution: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃. If 0.20 mol of AgNO₃ and 0.15 mol of NaCl are used, what is left over?
questions.x: The ratio is 1 : 1, so 0.15 mol NaCl (limiting) reacts with 0.15 mol AgNO₃, leaving 0.20 − 0.15 = 0.05 mol AgNO₃.

questions.q: In an ammonia reactor, 1 mol of N₂ and 6 mol of H₂ react completely according to N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. How many moles of H₂ are left over?
questions.x: 1 mol N₂ is limiting and reacts with 3 mol H₂, so 6 − 3 = 3 mol H₂ remains. 5 mol assumes a 1 : 1 ratio.

questions.q: The (n + l) value of a 4f subshell is:
questions.x: For 4f, n = 4 and l = 3, so n + l = 7. This is why 4f fills after 6s (n + l = 6).

questions.q: How many orbitals are present in a p subshell?
questions.x: For l = 1, m can be −1, 0 or +1, giving three p orbitals (px, py, pz). An s subshell has 1, d has 5 and f has 7.

questions.q: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C. At constant pressure, at what temperature would its volume theoretically be 100 cm³?
questions.x: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature: 27 °C = 300 K, and one-third of that is 100 K, which is −173 °C. Dividing 27 °C by 3 gives the wrong 9 °C.

questions.q: A gas bubble rises from the bottom of a lake, where the pressure is 3 atm, to the surface, where it is 1 atm. If the temperature stays the same, its volume:
questions.x: By Boyle's law, volume is inversely proportional to pressure. The pressure falls to one-third, so the volume becomes three times larger.

questions.q: A 2 dm³ flask of a gas at 3 atm is connected to a 4 dm³ flask of the same gas at 1.5 atm. The temperature stays constant. The final pressure is:
questions.x: Total PV = (3 × 2) + (1.5 × 4) = 12 dm³ atm, shared over 6 dm³, so P = 12/6 = 2 atm. Simply averaging the two pressures gives the wrong 2.25 atm.

questions.q: Which of the following temperatures is NOT possible?
questions.x: Nothing can be colder than absolute zero, about −273 °C. −300 °C lies below it, so it is impossible; −270 °C is about 3 K.

questions.q: At 1 atm, diethyl ether boils at 35 °C, ethanol at 78 °C and water at 100 °C. At 25 °C, the order of their vapour pressures is:
questions.x: A lower boiling point means weaker intermolecular forces and a higher vapour pressure at any given temperature, so ether > ethanol > water.

questions.q: Which shows the coordination numbers (cation : anion) in the sodium chloride and caesium chloride crystals correctly?
questions.x: In NaCl each ion has 6 nearest neighbours of opposite charge; in CsCl each ion has 8, because the larger Cs⁺ gives a larger radius ratio.

questions.q: Which of the following forms an ionic crystal?
questions.x: KBr is made of K⁺ and Br⁻ ions. Ice, sucrose and naphthalene are made of molecules and form molecular crystals.

questions.q: At chemical equilibrium, which quantity is zero?
o: The rate of the forward reaction
The rate of the reverse reaction
questions.x: Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so the net rate (forward minus reverse) is zero. Neither individual rate is zero.

questions.q: Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and Ksp of Ag₂CrO₄ is 1.1 × 10⁻¹². Which statement about their molar solubilities in water is correct?
o: AgCl is more soluble, since its Ksp value is larger
Both are equally soluble, since both are silver salts
Ag₂CrO₄ is more soluble, since Ksp = 4s³ gives the larger s
Neither dissolves at all, since both Ksp values are tiny
questions.x: AgCl: s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻⁵. Ag₂CrO₄: s = ∛(1.1 × 10⁻¹²/4) ≈ 6.5 × 10⁻⁵, so Ag₂CrO₄ is more soluble. Ksp values compare solubility directly only for salts of the same formula type.

questions.q: A catalyst is still needed in the Haber process at 400–500 °C because:
o: The strong N≡N triple bond gives the reaction a high activation energy
The catalyst increases the yield of ammonia
Hydrogen does not react with anything without it
questions.x: Breaking the very strong N≡N bond needs a lot of energy, so the reaction is slow even when hot; the iron catalyst lowers the activation energy. It does not change the yield.

questions.q: The concentration of a product rises from 0 to 0.12 mol dm⁻³ in the first 2 minutes. The average rate of formation of the product is:
questions.x: 2 minutes = 120 s, so rate = 0.12/120 = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. 0.06 is the rate per minute, not per second.

questions.q: For 2NO + 2H₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O, the experimental rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. Which conclusion is correct?
o: The order with respect to H₂ is 2, the same as its coefficient
The order with respect to H₂ is 1, although its coefficient in the equation is 2
The reaction is fourth order overall
The reaction is second order overall
questions.x: The powers in a rate equation come from experiment and need not match the coefficients. Here the order is 2 for NO and 1 for H₂, so 3 overall.

questions.q: Which statement about the laws of thermodynamics is correct?
o: They were derived from the structure of the atom
They are based on experience and do not depend on any theory of atomic structure
They apply only to chemical reactions, not to physical changes
They can predict the time a reaction takes
questions.x: The laws of thermodynamics summarise experience with bulk matter. They hold whatever theory of atoms is used, but say nothing about reaction time.

questions.q: Nitrogen dioxide can be made from the elements in two steps: forming 2 mol NO absorbs 180 kJ, then oxidising those 2 mol NO to 2 mol NO₂ releases 114 kJ. What is ΔH for N₂ + 2O₂ → 2NO₂ directly?
questions.x: Adding the two steps gives the direct route, so by Hess's law ΔH = +180 + (−114) = +66 kJ.

questions.q: A spontaneous process left to itself is:
o: Reversible at every stage without outside help
Unidirectional, moving towards a state of equilibrium
Always accompanied by a decrease in volume
questions.x: Spontaneous processes go in one natural direction until equilibrium is reached; they do not reverse by themselves.

questions.q: In the classical definition (in terms of oxygen and hydrogen), reduction is:
o: Addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen
Addition of oxygen and of hydrogen
Removal of both oxygen and hydrogen
Removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen
questions.x: Classically, reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen; oxidation is the reverse (gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen).

questions.q: Comparing the ions Zn²⁺ (E° −0.76 V) and Ag⁺ (E° +0.80 V), which conclusion about their oxidising power holds?
o: Zn²⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than Ag⁺
Silver is a stronger reducing agent than zinc
Zn²⁺ and Ag⁺ are equally strong oxidising agents
Ag⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than Zn²⁺
questions.x: A more positive E° means the ion is more easily reduced, so Ag⁺ is the stronger oxidising agent; zinc is the stronger reducing agent.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid (acetic acid), CH₃COOH, contains how many σ and π bonds in total?
questions.x: σ bonds: three C–H, one C–C, one in C=O, one C–O and one O–H = 7. Only the C=O double bond has a π bond, so there is 1 π.

questions.q: Which molecule has the strongest bond between its two atoms?
questions.x: N₂ has a triple bond (one σ, two π), O₂ a double bond, and F₂ and Cl₂ only single bonds. More bonds between the same pair of atoms means a higher bond energy.

questions.q: In gaseous mercury(II) chloride, HgCl₂, mercury has two bond pairs and no lone pair. The shape of the molecule is:
questions.x: Two bond pairs with no lone pair repel each other to opposite sides, giving a linear molecule with a 180° angle. A bent shape needs lone pairs on the central atom.

questions.q: Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, yet its electron affinity is less negative. The reason is that:
o: Fluorine has a smaller nuclear charge than chlorine
Fluorine already has a complete octet
The incoming electron enters the 3d subshell of fluorine
The small, crowded 2p subshell of F repels an incoming electron strongly
questions.x: In the very small fluorine atom, electron–electron repulsion in the compact 2p subshell partly cancels the attraction for an added electron.

questions.q: How many groups (vertical columns) make up the p-block of the periodic table?
questions.x: A p subshell holds 6 electrons, so the p-block is 6 columns wide. The s-block has 2, the d-block 10 and the f-block 14.

questions.q: Which compound is correctly matched with its class?
questions.x: Cyclobutane is a carbon-only ring that behaves like an alkane. Benzene is homocyclic aromatic, pyridine has a nitrogen in its ring, and propane is open-chain.

questions.q: Bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br, belongs to the class of:
questions.x: Replacing a hydrogen of an alkane by a halogen atom gives a haloalkane; the halogen atom is the functional group.

questions.q: 2-bromobutane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃, is heated with alcoholic KOH. The major product is:
questions.x: H can be lost from either neighbouring carbon, but the more substituted alkene, but-2-ene, is the major product. Butan-2-ol would form with aqueous KOH.

questions.q: Which type of bond breaking produces ions rather than free radicals?
o: Homolytic fission, where each atom takes one bonding electron
Homolytic fission, where neither atom takes an electron
Heterolytic fission, where each atom takes one bonding electron
Heterolytic fission, where one atom takes both bonding electrons
questions.x: In heterolytic fission both shared electrons go to one atom, giving a positive and a negative ion. Homolytic fission shares the electrons equally and gives free radicals.

questions.q: The organic product of the sulphonation of benzene is:
questions.x: Benzene reacts with fuming H₂SO₄ to replace one H atom by –SO₃H, giving benzenesulphonic acid.

questions.q: Name this branched alkyne by the IUPAC system: HC≡C–CH₂–CH(CH₃)₂
questions.x: The longest chain containing the triple bond has five carbons. Numbering from the ≡CH end gives the triple bond position 1 and the methyl group position 4.

questions.q: The simplest alkene after ethene, CH₃CH=CH₂, has the IUPAC name:
questions.x: A three-carbon chain with one C=C bond is propene. Numbering from the end nearer the double bond gives 1, so no locant is needed; prop-2-ene numbers from the wrong end.

questions.q: A component of petrol has the condensed formula (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂CH₃. Following IUPAC rules, this compound is named:
questions.x: The longest chain has five carbons, and numbering from the end nearer the branch puts the methyl group on carbon 2. 4-methylpentane numbers from the wrong end.

questions.q: How many σ and π bonds are present in buta-1,3-diene, CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂?
questions.x: There are six C–H σ bonds and three C–C σ bonds, making 9 σ. Each of the two double bonds also contains one π bond, giving 2 π.

questions.q: Chloroethane, bromoethane and iodoethane have the same alkyl group. Their boiling points increase in the order:
questions.x: Heavier, larger halogens give larger molecules with stronger London (van der Waals) forces, so the boiling point rises from the chloro to the iodo compound.

questions.q: Which carbon–halogen bond is the shortest?
questions.x: Fluorine has the smallest atomic radius of the halogens, so the C–F bond is the shortest. The bond length increases down the group to C–I.

questions.q: Allyl alcohol, CH₂=CHCH₂OH, is called in the IUPAC system:
questions.x: The –OH group gets the lowest number, so the carbon carrying it is C-1 and the double bond starts at C-2: prop-2-en-1-ol. 'Prop-1-en-3-ol' numbers from the wrong end.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through an aqueous solution of sodium phenoxide. What happens?
o: Nothing, because phenol is a stronger acid than carbonic acid
Sodium phenoxide is oxidised to benzoic acid
Phenol is set free, because carbonic acid is a stronger acid than phenol
Phenol is converted into sodium benzoate
questions.x: Phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid, so CO₂ and water displace it: C₆H₅ONa + CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + NaHCO₃. This is also why phenol does not liberate CO₂ from NaHCO₃.

questions.q: Propyne, CH₃C≡CH, is hydrated using dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄. The main product is:
questions.x: By Markovnikov's rule the –OH of the enol goes to the middle carbon, CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which rearranges to the ketone CH₃COCH₃. Only ethyne gives an aldehyde by this method.

questions.q: The arrangement of the three atoms bonded to the carbonyl carbon of propanone is:
o: Tetrahedral, with bond angles of about 109.5°
Trigonal planar, with bond angles of about 120°
Linear, with a bond angle of 180°
Pyramidal, with bond angles of about 107°
questions.x: The carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridised, so its three σ bonds lie in one plane at about 120°. The π bond lies above and below that plane.

questions.q: 3.0 g of ethanoic acid (Mr 60) is added to excess sodium carbonate: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + CO₂ + H₂O. What volume of CO₂ is formed at STP? (1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: Moles of acid = 3.0/60 = 0.05; CO₂ = 0.05/2 = 0.025 mol; 0.025 × 22.4 = 0.56 dm³. Ignoring the 2 : 1 ratio gives 1.12 dm³.

questions.q: The enzyme diastase (amylase) acts on starch, giving mainly:
questions.x: Diastase hydrolyses starch into maltose, which maltase can then split into glucose. Glucose and fructose come from sucrose by invertase.

questions.q: Polyester fibres repel water and are difficult to dye. They are usually dyed with:
questions.x: Disperse dyes are almost insoluble in water and are applied as a fine dispersion that dissolves into the hydrophobic polyester. Direct dyes are for cotton and acid dyes for wool, silk and nylon.

questions.q: A particle is pulled by a 12 N force due east and a 5 N force due north. How large is the net pull on it?
questions.x: The forces are perpendicular, so R = √(12² + 5²) = √169 = 13 N. 17 N would be correct only if the forces acted in the same direction.

questions.q: When a rifle fires a bullet, the bullet gets much more kinetic energy than the rifle because:
o: The bullet gets more momentum than the rifle
The rifle gets no momentum at all
Both get equal momentum, and kinetic energy p²/2m is larger for the smaller mass
Kinetic energy is shared equally between them
questions.x: The rifle and bullet get equal and opposite momenta. Since KE = p²/2m, the bullet with its much smaller mass gets far more kinetic energy.

questions.q: A 60 kg man stands on a weighing machine in an elevator that is moving upward but slowing down at 2 m s⁻². Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the machine reads:
questions.x: Slowing while moving up means the acceleration is 2 m s⁻² downward. R = m(g − a) = 60 × 8 = 480 N. 720 N would apply if the elevator were speeding up while going up.

questions.q: Two balls are thrown horizontally from the top of the same tower with speeds of 5 m s⁻¹ and 10 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance, the ratio of their horizontal distances from the tower on landing is:
questions.x: Both fall the same height, so they take the same time. Horizontal distance = speed × time, so the distances are in the ratio 5 : 10 = 1 : 2.

questions.q: A train's velocity increases uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ to 20 m s⁻¹ over a distance of 75 m. Its acceleration is:
questions.x: v² = u² + 2as gives 400 = 100 + 2a × 75, so 150a = 300 and a = 2 m s⁻². 4 m s⁻² forgets the factor 2.

questions.q: The velocity of a body changes uniformly from 6 m s⁻¹ to 14 m s⁻¹ along a straight line. Its average velocity during this change is:
questions.x: For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (initial + final) ÷ 2 = (6 + 14) ÷ 2 = 10 m s⁻¹. 8 m s⁻¹ is the change in velocity.

questions.q: Momentum and kinetic energy in a perfectly elastic collision (no external force): which are conserved?
o: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
questions.x: Momentum is conserved in every collision without external force. In a perfectly elastic collision, kinetic energy is also conserved.

questions.q: A boy does 600 J of work in 2 minutes. His average power is:
questions.x: P = W/t = 600 ÷ 120 s = 5 W. Using 2 instead of 120 s gives the wrong answer of 300 W.

questions.q: A 10 g bullet moving at 200 m s⁻¹ penetrates 0.1 m into a wooden block and stops. The average resistive force of the wood is:
questions.x: KE = ½ × 0.01 × 200² = 200 J. This is used up as work against the wood: F × 0.1 = 200, so F = 2000 N.

questions.q: In a solar cell, the main energy change is from:
questions.x: A solar (photovoltaic) cell absorbs light and produces an electric current, so it converts light energy into electrical energy.

questions.q: For a particle in uniform circular motion, which statement about directions is correct?
o: Both linear and angular velocity are along the tangent
Linear velocity is along the tangent; angular velocity is along the axis
Linear velocity is along the radius; angular velocity is along the tangent
Both linear and angular velocity point towards the centre
questions.x: The linear velocity is tangent to the circle, while angular velocity is a vector along the axis of rotation, given by the right-hand rule.

questions.q: A skydiver falling at terminal velocity opens her parachute. What happens next?
o: She speeds up until she reaches a higher terminal velocity
She stops falling for a moment and then falls at the old speed
She slows down until she reaches a new, lower terminal velocity
She keeps falling at the same terminal velocity
questions.x: The parachute greatly increases the drag, so drag exceeds weight and the net force is upward. She decelerates; as her speed falls the drag falls, until drag again equals weight at a lower terminal velocity.

questions.q: On a gusty day, the wind near the ground keeps changing its speed and direction from moment to moment. This wind is an example of:
questions.x: A velocity at a point that keeps changing irregularly is the mark of turbulent flow. Laminar and steady flow have smooth, unchanging velocities.

questions.q: A liquid flows through a pipe that has a small leak halfway along. The equation A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ between the two ends no longer holds because:
o: The liquid becomes compressible at the leak
The density of the liquid doubles
Some mass leaves through the leak, so the mass entering one end no longer equals the mass leaving the other
questions.x: Continuity expresses conservation of mass between two sections with nothing gained or lost between them. A leak removes mass in between, so the two flow rates differ.

questions.q: Water enters a pipe at 1.5 m s⁻¹ through a cross-section of area 6 cm² and leaves at 4.5 m s⁻¹. The cross-sectional area at the exit is:
questions.x: A₂ = A₁v₁/v₂ = 6 × 1.5 / 4.5 = 2 cm². Multiplying instead of dividing gives the wrong 18 cm².

questions.q: In a longitudinal wave, a rarefaction is a part of the medium in which:
o: The particles are farther apart and the pressure is lower than normal
The particles are closest together and the pressure is highest
The particles have their largest sideways displacement
There are no particles at all
questions.x: A rarefaction is a stretched region: particles are spread out, so density and pressure fall below normal. The crowded, high-pressure region is a compression.

questions.q: Two solids have the same density, but the elastic modulus of one is 4 times that of the other. The speed of sound in the stiffer solid is:
questions.x: v = √(E/ρ); with ρ the same, v ∝ √E, so 4 times the modulus gives √4 = 2 times the speed.

questions.q: The length of a simple pendulum is increased by 21%. Its time period increases by:
questions.x: T ∝ √l, so the new period is √1.21 = 1.1 times the old one, an increase of 10%.

questions.q: Dolphins use ultrasound under water. These ultrasound waves are:
questions.x: Ultrasound is sound of very high frequency, so like all sound in a fluid it is a longitudinal mechanical wave. Electromagnetic waves are always transverse.

questions.q: In a ripple tank, a dipper vibrates at 10 Hz. The distance from the first crest to the sixth crest is 10 cm. The speed of the ripples is:
questions.x: Six crests span 5 wavelengths, so λ = 10/5 = 2 cm. v = fλ = 10 × 2 = 20 cm s⁻¹.

questions.q: Yellow light has a wavelength of 600 nm in a vacuum. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, its frequency is:
3 mol of an ideal gas with Cp = 29 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is heated at constant pressure through 10 K. The heat supplied is:
questions.x: Q = nCpΔT = 3 × 29 × 10 = 870 J. Forgetting the number of moles gives 290 J.

questions.q: A gas at pressure P pushes a piston of area A outward through a small distance Δx. The result W = PΔV follows from:
o: Work = force PA × distance Δx, and AΔx is the change in volume
questions.x: The gas exerts force F = PA on the piston. W = FΔx = PAΔx, and AΔx is the volume swept, ΔV, so W = PΔV.

questions.q: Two charges, each +q, are placed a distance 2a apart. The magnitude of the net electric field at a point on their perpendicular bisector, at a distance a from the midpoint, is:
questions.x: Each charge is a√2 away, giving kq/2a². The components along the bisector add: 2 × (kq/2a²) × cos 45° = kq/(√2 a²); the other components cancel.

questions.q: The electric potential at point P is 250 V. The electric potential energy of a charge of −2 μC placed at P is:
questions.x: U = qV = (−2 × 10⁻⁶) × 250 = −5 × 10⁻⁴ J. The sign of the charge must be kept; dividing V by q gives a meaningless huge number.

questions.q: A fixed point charge of +4 nC is in vacuum. How much work is needed to bring a charge of +2 μC slowly from infinity to a point 0.6 m from it? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
The field lines of a single isolated positive point charge are:
o: Straight lines radiating outward in all directions
Straight lines pointing inward from all directions
questions.x: For an isolated positive charge, the lines are radial and point away from it. Inward-pointing lines belong to a negative charge; parallel lines show a uniform field.

questions.q: A lamp draws a current of 0.25 A from a 230 V supply. Its resistance while working is:
questions.x: R = V/I = 230 ÷ 0.25 = 920 Ω. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 57.5.

questions.q: A square loop of side 20 cm is held with its plane at right angles to a uniform field of 0.5 T. The flux through it is:
questions.x: A = 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04 m², so Φ = BA = 0.5 × 0.04 = 0.02 Wb. Forgetting to square the side gives 0.1 Wb.

questions.q: A loop has its normal along a uniform field. The field is doubled and the loop is tilted so its normal is at 60° to the field. The flux through the loop (cos 60° = 0.5):
questions.x: New flux = 2B × A × cos 60° = 2B × A × 0.5 = BA, the same as before.

questions.q: A 100-turn coil of resistance 10 Ω is part of a closed circuit. The flux through each turn changes by 0.01 Wb in 0.5 s. The induced current in the coil is:
questions.x: ε = N ΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 0.01/0.5 = 2 V, so I = ε/R = 2/10 = 0.2 A. Stopping at the emf gives the tempting 2.

questions.q: A capacitor in a circuit lets an alternating current flow but not a steady direct current. This is because with AC the capacitor:
o: Lets electrons pass through its insulating layer
Charges and discharges repeatedly, so charge keeps moving in the circuit
Has zero reactance at every frequency
questions.x: No charge crosses the dielectric. With AC the plates are charged and discharged each half-cycle, so current flows in the wires; with steady DC it stops once charged.

questions.q: A full-wave rectifier is built from a centre-tapped transformer and two diodes. At any moment while the load carries current, how many of these diodes are conducting?
o: It alternates between none and two
questions.x: In the centre-tapped circuit the two diodes take turns: one conducts during the positive half-cycle and the other during the negative half-cycle, so only one conducts at a time.

questions.q: When the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is plotted against frequency, the point where the straight line cuts the frequency axis gives the:
questions.x: KEmax = hf − hf₀ is zero when f = f₀, so the line meets the frequency axis at the threshold frequency. Its slope, not its intercept, is h.

questions.q: Which of these sources gives a bright-line emission spectrum?
o: The glowing filament of a tungsten lamp
Neon gas glowing in a discharge tube
questions.x: A low-pressure gas of separate atoms, excited electrically, emits only its own characteristic wavelengths. Hot solids and liquids give continuous spectra.

questions.q: Which relation between the decay constant λ and the half-life T½ is correct?
questions.x: λ T½ = ln 2 = 0.693, so λ = 0.693/T½. A larger decay constant means a shorter half-life.

questions.q: A college asked 200 of its students how they travel to classes. Ninety said they walk, sixty come by bus and thirty ride motorbikes. All the others are dropped off by car. Of the bus users, one third said the buses are often late. According to the passage, how many students are dropped off by car?
questions.x: 90 + 60 + 30 = 180 students use the other ways, so 200 - 180 = 20 are dropped off by car.

questions.q: "A deafening silence filled the ward as the surgeon walked in." The phrase 'deafening silence' is an example of:
questions.x: An oxymoron puts two opposite ideas side by side; silence cannot literally be deafening. There is no comparison with 'like' or 'as', so it is not a simile.

questions.q: Which sentence places the modifier so that the meaning is clear and sensible?
o: Ali found a gold watch walking in the park.
While walking in the park, Ali found a gold watch.
Walking in the park, a gold watch caught Ali's eye.
A gold watch was found walking in the park by Ali.
questions.x: The modifier 'walking in the park' must sit next to the person doing the walking; in the other sentences it seems to describe the watch.

questions.q: Which sentence places 'usually' correctly?
o: We usually have dinner at eight.
We have usually dinner at eight.
We have dinner at usually eight.
We usually dinner have at eight.
questions.x: An adverb of frequency such as 'usually' normally comes before the main verb, here 'have', and never between a verb and its object.

questions.q: Choose the direct form of: The teacher asked Bilal whether he had brought his notebook.
o: The teacher said to Bilal, "You have brought your notebook."
The teacher said to Bilal, "Have you brought your notebook?"
The teacher said to Bilal, "Has he brought his notebook?"
The teacher said to Bilal, "Have you brought his notebook?"
questions.x: The reported 'had brought' goes back to the present perfect 'have brought', and 'he/his' become 'you/your' because the teacher speaks to Bilal. The direct form must also be a question, not a statement.

questions.q: Choose the correct pronoun: "Sara painted the whole room ___, without anyone's help."
questions.x: The antecedent 'Sara' is singular and female, so the reflexive or emphatic pronoun is 'herself'.

questions.q: Change into the passive voice: "The workers are building a new hospital."
o: A new hospital was being built by the workers.
A new hospital is built by the workers.
A new hospital has been built by the workers.
A new hospital is being built by the workers.
questions.x: The present continuous passive is 'is/are being' + past participle.

questions.q: "Although the chief guest had promised a short speech, he was so verbose that the audience waited two hours for lunch." The word 'verbose' means:
questions.x: 'Verbose' means using more words than needed; 'although ... short speech' sets up the contrast with a speech that went on for two hours.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "Unless you do not revise regularly, you will forget the formulas."
o: Unless you will revise regularly, you will forget the formulas.
Unless you not revise regularly, you will forget the formulas.
Unless you do not revise regularly, you forget the formulas.
Unless you revise regularly, you will forget the formulas.
questions.x: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so adding 'do not' makes a double negative that reverses the meaning. The verb after 'unless' stays in the present simple.

questions.q: A doctor advises a patient to stop smoking. The patient replies, "You smoke too, so your advice is wrong." Why is the patient's reply a false argument?
o: Doctors are not allowed to smoke
The patient has not smoked for very long
The doctor did not give any advice
Whether the doctor smokes does not change whether the advice is correct
questions.x: The advice is right or wrong on the evidence about smoking. Pointing out that the adviser does the same thing does not answer the advice.

questions.q: Statement: Should candidates be allowed to bring calculators into the entry test? Argument I: Yes, all students like using calculators. Argument II: No, calculators are made in other countries. Which argument is strong?
o: Neither argument I nor II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
questions.x: Liking something is not a reason to allow it, and where a calculator is made has nothing to do with fair testing. Neither argument is strong.

questions.q: Find the missing term: AC, EG, ?, MO, QS
questions.x: Each pair skips one letter (A_C, E_G) and the next pair starts 4 letters later: A, E, I, M, Q. So the missing pair is IK.

questions.q: Find the next number: 5, -10, 20, -40, ?
questions.x: Each term is multiplied by -2: -40 x -2 = 80. The sign changes every step.

questions.q: Hina, Iqra, Javeria, Kiran, Laiba and Mehwish sit in a row facing north. Kiran is at the right end. Hina is second from the left, and Laiba sits immediately to Hina's right. Mehwish sits next to Kiran. Javeria is not at an end. Who sits immediately to the left of Mehwish?
questions.x: Seats from the left: Hina 2, Laiba 3, Kiran 6, and Mehwish 5 (next to Kiran). Javeria cannot be at an end, so she takes seat 4 and Iqra seat 1. Seat 4, Javeria, is left of Mehwish.

questions.q: Ali can paint a wall in 6 hours, and Bilal can paint the same kind of wall in 3 hours. They paint one wall together, and then Ali alone paints a second, identical wall. How many hours does the whole job take?
questions.x: Together they paint 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 of a wall per hour, so the first wall takes 2 hours. Ali alone needs 6 hours for the second: 2 + 6 = 8 hours.

questions.q: Statement: Bilal's car engine overheats whenever he drives in summer, and the mechanic found that the coolant level is very low. Courses of action: I. Bilal should have the coolant refilled and the system checked for leaks. II. Bilal should sell the car at once. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: The information points to the low coolant, so refilling it and checking for leaks is the sensible decision. Selling the car ignores a simple fix.

questions.q: Statement: Patients at a rural health centre wait for hours because only one doctor visits, and only on three days a week. Courses of action: I. More doctors should be posted to the centre, or the doctor's working days increased. II. The centre should be closed because it is of little use. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: The problem is too little doctor time, so adding doctors or days solves it. Closing the centre would leave patients with no care at all.

questions.q: Statement I: Many people in the city suffered from heatstroke last week. Statement II: Demand for electricity in the city reached a record high last week. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: Heatstroke does not raise electricity demand, and demand does not cause heatstroke. A severe heatwave would explain both.
